sorry to immediately upset you by admitting that I voted to remain, *but* upon my first entrance into the polling station I felt such disgust at the non-democratic federalist leaders of the union being responsible for our affairs that I didn't at that point feel able to go through with my intention to vote remain. I went to have a little sleep and some food so that I could think clearly and feel good about voting remain. I was only able to rationalise it by the fact that remaining in, we would have given far more problems to the federalists than we will leaving and inviting them to take advantage of us at leisure. we have now taken away a road-block to dominance in the region and in addition the union will try to make an example of us to avoid contagion if they possibly can. So I voted in and I am proud to have done so, but having gone through the emotions that I did, I thought that the majority of people who felt the same way would just vote leave. you can't put a price on sovereignty, and while I was voting for staying in and undermining their project, I can understand why leave won. The remain arguments made were too defensive, too complementary to the federalist non-democratic mess. I realise this is because, if they had won, they needed to keep their place in the poker game but *somebody* needed to come out and go off-message with more cynical reasons to vote in. A prominent politician would have been perfect, as he is leaving politics anyway so what would it matter to him if it made him a pariah in the union and unemployable in domestic politics for that reason? A cynical argument could have persuaded many people who, like me, felt a strong *strong* urge to say NO to the leaders who think that it is acceptable to run the union the way they do but, unlike me, thought the best way to achieve that was to vote leave.

and perhaps I was wrong. I was assuming that if, after a close vote, the many promises made by remain were proven to be false, there would surely be another referendum and an out vote, meaning that to go nuclear this time was premature. but perhaps this was indeed the last chance to escape the federal project, in which case the collective wisdom would have got it right. unlike a general election, however, we are dealing with "foreigners" who most citizens don't really understand culturally. this lack of an "informed" gut I think may undermine the foundations upon which the soundness of our democratic decisions lie.

They are very different singers. I love, love, *love* a famous tenor - he is truly remarkable. But I prefer him in roles like Otello (obviously), Chenier (so unbelievably awesome in this role), and Turiddu. Compared to another renowned tenor, he has a higher voice that gains extra power and strength through excellent technique and wonderful emotion, whereas the other tenor has more power and achieves his extended top through wonderful technique and emotion/acting, and for the role of Calaf, I think the latter type of singer just works better.

The role is meant for a huge voice with easy power more than a high voice that can generate power. You have to listen to how they sing non piangere liu, and also the other tenor's riddle scene with a famous soprano as Turandot just can't be bettered. Manrico is another role where I think the other tenor's grand voice favors him over the first tenor. However, I think that not having such easy power is an advantage for the first tenor in roles like Otello. I think a reason that the other tenor did not sing this role was that he would not have been able to compete with the interpretation of the first tenor because the other tenor didn't need to be "unhinged" or particularly shout to sing the outbursts. But they *shouldn't* be easy because Otello is meant to be going through intense emotional turmoil, and it sounds wrong if they are easy like that. He would have had trouble with this, I think.

Another example of this is a well-known baritone as Iago. I love love love him, but as Iago he can't generate any electricity because the power is too easy for him and he sounds too noble. He is fantastic as Don Carlo in a famous opera, though, because that role really *really* benefits from the way he can sing all the really powerful passages while still sounding like a nobleman. The character of Enrico Ashton, too.

Anyway. Please at least give the other tenor a chance singing "Ah, si ben mio" (from a well-known opera) - it's just out of this world.... and for goodness' sake don't judge him by his performance as Rodolfo, which he shouldn't have done in my opinion.

There is a direct physical link between the vibrations in the recording environment and the vibrations of your eardrums.
